title: Fifth commandment: health (CCC 2288–2301)
hook: care for health, and respect for the dead

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth commandment from Cain's field: every life is sacred, and peace starts with anger. Your line was every life. Did you take your small step toward peace? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-nine.

Goal reached, ten thousand steps, says the wristband. Down the street, another person hasn't seen a doctor in six years and jokes that the body will let him know. And in an old story from the Bible, a man named Tobit leaves his dinner untasted, goes out, and carries home the body of a murdered man lying in the street, so he can bury him after sunset. Three ways of treating a body. Yesterday the fifth commandment guarded life. Today it turns to the body itself, living and dead.
screen: `A WRISTBAND BUZZES.` → `SIX YEARS WITHOUT A DOCTOR.` → `TOBIT LEAVES HIS DINNER.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says life and physical health are precious gifts entrusted to us by God. So we're asked to take reasonable care of them, keeping in mind the needs of others and the common good. And it adds a line about society: it should help people find food, clothing, housing, health care, schooling and work. Health, in that picture, is never only private. Then it says something sharp in the other direction. Morality respects bodily life, but it doesn't make it an absolute. The Catechism rejects what it calls a cult of the body: sacrificing everything for it, idolizing physical perfection and success at sports. The body is a gift to care for, not a god to serve. In between, it names the virtue of temperance: avoiding every kind of excess, the abuse of food, alcohol, tobacco or medicine. And it says plainly that those who put others in danger, by drunkenness or reckless speed, are gravely guilty. Using drugs, except on strictly medical grounds, it calls a grave offense. Then the Catechism follows the body all the way to the end. The dying, it says, should be given attention and care, to help them live their last moments in dignity and peace, and surrounded by prayer. And the bodies of the dead must be treated with respect and charity, in faith and hope of the resurrection. Burying the dead, it says, is a work of mercy. That's Tobit, leaving his dinner to carry a dead man home. The Catechism also says organ donation after death can be a noble act, and that cremation is permitted, as long as it isn't chosen as a denial of faith in the resurrection. So the line runs from the gym to the graveside: care for the body, honor it, but don't worship it.
screen: `HEALTH: A GIFT ENTRUSTED.` · `NOT A CULT OF THE BODY.` · `TEMPERANCE: NO EXCESS.` · `THE DEAD, TREATED WITH RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take care of your body today. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet and move slowly upward, noticing each part without judging it. Where is there tension, tiredness, hunger, pain? Choose one small, reasonable kindness you can do for your body today: a glass of water, a walk, an early night, the appointment you keep putting off. If you pray, you can thank God for this body as a gift. If you don't, just thank it, plainly, for carrying you this far. The bell holds the time.
Fifth commandment. Respect for life includes reasonable care for health, temperance, and respect for the dying and the dead, without making the body an idol. Today's word.
Your line: care, not worship. Today, do the one kindness for your body you chose, and skip one thing you do only for how it looks. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics are taught to care for their health with temperance, to accompany the dying with prayer and the sacraments, and to bury the dead with a funeral Mass, a corporal work of mercy.

fork.setup: you're Tobit, sitting down to a good dinner. word comes that a murdered man's body is lying in the street. what do you do?
options: finish your dinner; it isn't your business.
get up, bring the body in, and bury it after dark.

fork.reveal: in the book of Tobit, he leaves his food, takes the body in, and buries it when the sun has set.

what it means: health is a gift to care for reasonably, never an idol, and the dying and the dead are owed respect.

Audit (y4 1122–1131): the Douay-Rheims calls the book and the man 'Tobias' (Tobias 2:1–9: he leaves his dinner, carries the slain man home privately, and buries him after sunset); the script uses the common name Tobit.
